questionText:
Given below is a chemical equation showing the reaction between magnesium ribbon and oxygen gas.
Mg(s) + O2(g) -> X
a. Identify the product X and balance the given chemical equation. (2 Marks)
b. Name the type of chemical reaction taking place in this equation. (1 Mark)
sloText: Identify types of chemical reactions and write balanced chemical equations.
checkingHints: Part a (2 marks): 1 mark for identifying product X as Magnesium oxide (MgO); 1 mark for balancing the equation: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s).
Part b (1 mark): Addition / synthesis / combination / combustion / oxidation reaction.

rubric.description: Part a: Identifies product X as Magnesium oxide (MgO).
Part a: Writes balanced chemical equation: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s).
Part b: Names reaction type as Addition / Synthesis / Combination / Combustion / Oxidation reaction.

modelAnswer:
a. Product Identification and Balanced Equation:
- Product X is Magnesium oxide (MgO).
- Balanced Chemical Equation:
  2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s)

b. Type of Chemical Reaction:
- Addition reaction (also known as a synthesis, combination, combustion, or oxidation-reduction reaction).

questionText:
Complete the table for the given substances (Draw Dot and Cross Diagram):
1. Oxygen gas (O2)
2. Nitrogen gas (N2)
3. Methane gas (CH4)
4. Carbon dioxide gas (CO2)
sloText: Draw dot and cross structures for simple covalent molecules containing single, double, and triple bonds.
checkingHints: 1 mark for each accurate dot-and-cross diagram showing all valence electrons (shared pairs and unshared lone pairs):
1. Oxygen gas (O2): Double covalent bond (2 shared pairs = 4 electrons) between two O atoms, with 2 lone pairs (4 electrons) on each O atom.
2. Nitrogen gas (N2): Triple covalent bond (3 shared pairs = 6 electrons) between two N atoms, with 1 lone pair (2 electrons) on each N atom.
3. Methane gas (CH4): Central C atom sharing 4 single covalent bonds (1 shared pair each) with four H atoms (no lone pairs).
4. Carbon dioxide gas (CO2): Central C atom forming two double covalent bonds (O=C=O; 2 shared pairs with each of the two O atoms), with 2 lone pairs on each O atom.

rubric.description: Draws O2 with a double bond (2 shared pairs) and 2 lone pairs on each oxygen atom.
Draws N2 with a triple bond (3 shared pairs) and 1 lone pair on each nitrogen atom.
Draws CH4 with 4 single C–H shared pairs around central carbon.
Draws CO2 with two C=O double bonds and 2 lone pairs on each oxygen atom.

modelAnswer:
Dot and Cross Structures of Covalent Molecules:
1. Oxygen gas (O2 — Double Covalent Bond):
   Each oxygen atom (Group VIA, 6 valence electrons) shares 2 electrons with the other to form a double covalent bond (O=O, 2 shared pairs), leaving 2 lone pairs (4 non-bonding electrons) on each oxygen atom.

2. Nitrogen gas (N2 — Triple Covalent Bond):
   Each nitrogen atom (Group VA, 5 valence electrons) shares 3 electrons with the other to form a triple covalent bond (N≡N, 3 shared pairs), leaving 1 lone pair (2 non-bonding electrons) on each nitrogen atom.

3. Methane gas (CH4 — Four Single Covalent Bonds):
   One central carbon atom (Group IVA, 4 valence electrons) shares 1 electron with each of four hydrogen atoms (1 valence electron each), forming four single covalent C–H bonds (no lone pairs).

4. Carbon dioxide gas (CO2 — Two Double Covalent Bonds):
   One central carbon atom (4 valence electrons) shares 2 electron pairs with each of the two oxygen atoms (O=C=O), forming two double covalent bonds while each oxygen atom retains 2 lone pairs.

questionText:
Consider the given structure of an atom of an element X (nucleus with 2 p, 2 n and 2 electrons in K shell) to answer the following questions.
a. Identify the element X. (1 Mark)
b. Name another element belonging to the same group as element X. (1 Mark)
c. State any THREE properties that all the elements of this group have in common. (3 Marks)
sloText: Identify elements from their atomic structures and describe the physical and chemical properties of Group VIIIA (noble gases).
checkingHints: Part a (1 mark): Helium (He).
Part b (1 mark): Any other Group VIIIA (Group 18) noble gas: Neon (Ne), Argon (Ar), Krypton (Kr), Xenon (Xe), or Radon (Rn).
Part c (3 marks - 1 mark for each of any 3 valid properties):
- All are colourless, odourless gases at room temperature and pressure.
- All exist as monoatomic gases.
- All have completely filled outermost valence shells (duplet for He, octet for others).
- All are chemically unreactive / inert (do not easily form ions or chemical bonds; zero valency).
- All have very high ionisation energies and very low melting and boiling points.

rubric.description: Part a: Identifies element X (Z = 2, A = 4) as Helium (He).
Part b: Names another Group VIIIA noble gas (Neon, Argon, Krypton, Xenon, or Radon).
Part c: States any 3 common properties of noble gases (1 mark each).

modelAnswer:
a. Element X has 2 protons, 2 neutrons, and 2 electrons; therefore, element X is Helium (He).

b. Another element belonging to the same group (Group VIIIA / Group 18, Noble Gases) is Neon (Ne) or Argon (Ar) (also acceptable: Krypton, Xenon, Radon).

c. Three Common Properties of Group VIIIA (Noble Gases):
1. Complete Valence Shell: All elements in this group possess a completely filled outermost electron shell (a duplet of 2 electrons in Helium and an octet of 8 electrons in all others).
2. Chemical Inertness (Zero Valency): Because their valence shells are complete, they are chemically unreactive (inert) and do not readily gain, lose, or share electrons to form compounds.
3. Monoatomic Colourless Gases: All exist as colourless, odourless, monoatomic gases at room temperature and pressure with very low melting and boiling points.

questionText:
a. i. State the relationship between volume and temperature of a gas presented by J. Charles. (1 Mark)
   ii. Give mathematical representation of Charles's law to support your answer in part i. (1 Mark)
b. A doctor prescribed milk of magnesia, a suspension of magnesium hydroxide, to a patient in order to be used as a neutraliser for stomach acidity.
   How would you determine that milk of magnesia is a suspension? Give THREE reasons. (3 Marks)
sloText: State Charles's law with its mathematical expression and describe the distinguishing properties of suspensions.
checkingHints: Part a.i (1 mark): The volume of a given mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute (Kelvin) temperature at constant pressure.
Part a.ii (1 mark): V ∝ T  or  V = kT  or  V / T = k  or  V1 / T1 = V2 / T2.
Part b (3 marks - 1 mark for each of any 3 distinguishing properties of a suspension):
1. Its particles are large (> 10^-5 cm or > 1000 nm in diameter) and visible to the naked eye.
2. It is a heterogeneous, cloudy/opaque mixture in which undissolved particles settle down upon standing.
3. Its solute particles cannot pass through ordinary filter paper and can be separated by filtration.
4. It blocks or scatters light (opaque appearance).

rubric.description: Part a.i: States that volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure.
Part a.ii: Writes mathematical expression V ∝ T, V/T = k, or V1/T1 = V2/T2.
Part b: Gives 3 experimental/physical reasons identifying milk of magnesia as a suspension (1 mark each).

modelAnswer:
a.i. Statement of Charles's Law:
Jacques Charles stated that the volume of a given mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (in Kelvin) provided the pressure is kept constant.

a.ii. Mathematical Representation of Charles's Law:
V ∝ T  (at constant P and n)
V = kT  =>  V / T = k
For two states: V1 / T1 = V2 / T2

b. Three Reasons Determining That Milk of Magnesia is a Suspension:
1. Heterogeneous & Settling on Standing: Milk of magnesia is a heterogeneous, milky/opaque mixture whose undissolved magnesium hydroxide particles settle down at the bottom of the bottle if left undisturbed (requiring shaking before use).
2. Large Particle Size Visible to Naked Eye: The suspended particles have diameters greater than 1000 nm (10^-5 cm), making them large enough to be seen with the naked eye or under a simple microscope.
3. Separation by Filtration: When milk of magnesia is poured through ordinary filter paper, the suspended magnesium hydroxide particles cannot pass through the pores and are retained on the filter paper as a solid residue.

questionText:
a. 150 cm3 of an aqueous sodium chloride solution contains 3 g sodium chloride. Calculate the mass/volume percentage of the given solution. (2 Marks)
b. If 15 cm3 of 5 M hydrochloric acid solution has been diluted to 100 cm3, then what will be the molarity of the prepared solution? (2 Marks)
sloText: Calculate percentage composition (% m/v) and perform molarity dilution calculations (M1V1 = M2V2).
checkingHints: Part a (2 marks):
- 1 mark for formula / substitution: % (m/v) = (Mass of solute in g / Volume of solution in cm3) × 100 = (3 / 150) × 100.
- 1 mark for correct answer: 2% (m/v).
Part b (2 marks):
- 1 mark for dilution formula / substitution: M1V1 = M2V2 => (5 M)(15 cm3) = M2(100 cm3).
- 1 mark for correct answer: M2 = 75 / 100 = 0.75 M.

rubric.description: Part a: Substitutes mass (3 g) and volume (150 cm3) into % (m/v) formula.
Part a: Calculates correct concentration of 2% (m/v).
Part b: Applies dilution equation M1V1 = M2V2 with M1=5, V1=15, V2=100.
Part b: Calculates final molarity M2 = 0.75 M.

modelAnswer:
a. Calculation of Mass/Volume Percentage (% m/v):
- Mass of solute (NaCl) = 3 g
- Volume of solution = 150 cm3
- Formula: % (m/v) = (Mass of solute (g) / Volume of solution (cm3)) × 100
- % (m/v) = (3 g / 150 cm3) × 100 = 2% (m/v)

b. Calculation of Molarity of Diluted HCl Solution:
- Initial Molarity (M1) = 5 M
- Initial Volume (V1) = 15 cm3
- Final Volume (V2) = 100 cm3
- Dilution Equation: M1V1 = M2V2
- M2 = (M1 × V1) / V2 = (5 M × 15 cm3) / 100 cm3 = 75 / 100 = 0.75 M

questionText:
An element X has relative atomic number of 11. It loses one electron and acquires +1 oxidation state. It gives a violent reaction with cold water.
a. Identify element X based on the given characteristics. (1 Mark)
b. Which period of the periodic table does element X belong to? (1 Mark)
c. What products are formed on reaction of element X with cold water? (2 Marks)
sloText: Identify alkali metals from atomic number and describe their position in the periodic table and reaction with water.
checkingHints: Part a (1 mark): Sodium (Na).
Part b (1 mark): Period 3 (3rd period).
Part c (2 marks): Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and Hydrogen gas (H2) — or balanced chemical equation: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 (1 mark for each product).

rubric.description: Part a: Identifies element X (Z = 11) as Sodium (Na).
Part b: Identifies Period 3 (since electronic configuration 2, 8, 1 has 3 shells).
Part c: Names or writes formulas for both products—Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and Hydrogen gas (H2).

modelAnswer:
a. Element X with atomic number 11 is Sodium (Na).

b. Electronic configuration of Sodium (Z = 11) is 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, 3s1 (K = 2, L = 8, M = 1). Since it has 3 occupied electron shells, it belongs to the 3rd Period (Period 3) of the periodic table.

c. When sodium reacts violently with cold water, the products formed are aqueous Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and Hydrogen gas (H2):
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)

questionText:
i. Mention any FOUR medical uses of isotopes of any element. (4 Marks)
ii. Draw the atomic structures of three isotopes of oxygen, specifying their number of protons, neutrons and electrons. (4 Marks)
sloText: Describe the uses of radioactive isotopes in medicine and draw the atomic structures of isotopes of elements.
checkingHints: Part i (4 marks - 1 mark for each of any 4 specific medical uses of radioisotopes):
1. Cobalt-60 (Co-60) emits strongly penetrating gamma rays used in radiotherapy to destroy internal malignant cancer tumours.
2. Phosphorus-32 (P-32) or Strontium-90 (Sr-90) emits less-penetrating beta radiation used to treat superficial skin cancer.
3. Iodine-131 (I-131) is used as a tracer to diagnose and treat thyroid gland disorders (goiter and thyroid cancer).
4. Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) is used for diagnostic imaging and monitoring bone growth and organ function.
5. Sodium-24 (Na-24) is injected into the bloodstream to trace blood circulation and detect blood clots or constriction.
Part ii (4 marks):
- Specifying p, e, and n counts for 16_8 O (p=8, e=8, n=8), 17_8 O (p=8, e=8, n=9), and 18_8 O (p=8, e=8, n=10) (1 mark).

- Drawing three Bohr atomic structures, each showing a central nucleus with the respective p and n counts surrounded by K-shell (2 electrons) and L-shell (6 electrons) (3 marks: 1 mark per isotope diagram).

rubric.description: Part i: States 4 distinct medical uses of radioactive isotopes (1 mark each).
Part ii: Specifies correct proton (8), electron (8), and neutron counts (8, 9, and 10) for the three oxygen isotopes.
Part ii: Draws accurate Bohr atomic structures for 16_8 O, 17_8 O, and 18_8 O with K=2 and L=6 electrons (1 mark each).

modelAnswer:
i. Four Medical Uses of Radioactive Isotopes:
1. Treatment of Internal Cancer (Cobalt-60): Cobalt-60 emits high-energy, strongly penetrating gamma rays that are directed at deep-seated malignant tumours to destroy cancer cells without surgery.
2. Treatment of Skin Cancer (Phosphorus-32 & Strontium-90): Isotopes of P-32 and Sr-90 emit less-penetrating beta (β) radiations, making them ideal for treating surface skin cancers without damaging deeper healthy tissues.
3. Diagnosis & Treatment of Thyroid Goiter (Iodine-131): Radioactive Iodine-131 is selectively absorbed by the thyroid gland and is used to diagnose and treat goiter and thyroid tumours.
4. Bone Growth & Circulatory Tracing (Technetium-99m & Sodium-24): Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) is used to monitor bone growth and fractures, while Sodium-24 (Na-24) is used to trace blood circulation and locate blood clots.

ii. Atomic Structures of the Three Isotopes of Oxygen:
Oxygen (Z = 8) has three natural isotopes: Oxygen-16 (16_8 O), Oxygen-17 (17_8 O), and Oxygen-18 (18_8 O).

1. Oxygen-16 (16_8 O):
   - Protons (p^+) = 8, Electrons (e^-) = 8, Neutrons (n^0) = 16 - 8 = 8.
   - Structure: Nucleus [p = 8, n = 8]; K-shell = 2 electrons; L-shell = 6 electrons.

2. Oxygen-17 (17_8 O):
   - Protons (p^+) = 8, Electrons (e^-) = 8, Neutrons (n^0) = 17 - 8 = 9.
   - Structure: Nucleus [p = 8, n = 9]; K-shell = 2 electrons; L-shell = 6 electrons.

3. Oxygen-18 (18_8 O):
   - Protons (p^+) = 8, Electrons (e^-) = 8, Neutrons (n^0) = 18 - 8 = 10.
   - Structure: Nucleus [p = 8, n = 10]; K-shell = 2 electrons; L-shell = 6 electrons.

questionText:
Given are the atomic structures of calcium and chlorine. These two elements form a compound called calcium chloride.
i. Name the bond that joins calcium and chlorine atoms together. (1 Mark)
ii. Explain the formation of bond between calcium and chlorine atoms. (6 Marks)
iii. Draw a dot and cross diagram to represent the bond in calcium chloride. (1 Mark)
sloText: Describe the formation of ionic bonds in binary compounds (such as CaCl2) using electronic configurations and dot-and-cross diagrams.
checkingHints: Part i (1 mark): Ionic bond (electrovalent bond).
Part ii (6 marks):
- Calcium (Z=20; 2, 8, 8, 2) is an electropositive metal with 2 valence electrons in its outermost N-shell (1.5 marks).
- Chlorine (Z=17; 2, 8, 7) is an electronegative non-metal with 7 valence electrons in its outermost M-shell, needing 1 electron to complete its octet (1.5 marks).
- One calcium atom loses its 2 valence electrons (one to each of two chlorine atoms) to form a stable Ca^(2+) cation (2, 8, 8) (1.5 marks).

- Two chlorine atoms each gain 1 electron to form two Cl^- anions (2, 8, 8), and the oppositely charged Ca^(2+) and 2Cl^- ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction to form CaCl2 (1.5 marks).
Part iii (1 mark):
- Draws accurate dot-and-cross representation: [Cl]^- [Ca]^(2+) [Cl]^- (or Ca^(2+) with two [ :Cl: ]^- anions showing 7 dots and 1 transferred cross).

rubric.description: Part i: Identifies the bond as an Ionic (or electrovalent) bond.
Part ii: Explains valence configurations of Ca (2,8,8,2) and Cl (2,8,7), transfer of 2 electrons from one Ca atom to two Cl atoms, formation of Ca^(2+) and 2Cl^- ions, and electrostatic attraction.
Part iii: Draws dot-and-cross diagram of CaCl2 showing [Ca]^(2+) and two [Cl]^- ions with complete octets.

modelAnswer:
i. Name of the Bond:
Ionic bond (or electrovalent bond).

ii. Explanation of Bond Formation in Calcium Chloride (CaCl2):
1. Electronic Configuration of Reacting Atoms:
   - Calcium (20_Ca) is an electropositive Group IIA metal with electronic configuration 2, 8, 8, 2 (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2). It has 2 electrons in its outermost valence shell.
   - Chlorine (17_Cl) is an electronegative Group VIIA non-metal with electronic configuration 2, 8, 7 (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5). It has 7 valence electrons and requires 1 more electron to complete its stable octet.
2. Complete Transfer of Electrons:
   - To achieve the stable noble gas configuration of Argon (2, 8, 8), one calcium atom loses its two 4s valence electrons, forming a divalent positively charged calcium cation:
     Ca (2, 8, 8, 2) -> Ca^(2+) (2, 8, 8) + 2e^-
   - Because each chlorine atom can accept only 1 electron, two chlorine atoms each gain one of the electrons lost by the calcium atom, forming two monovalent negatively charged chloride anions:
     2Cl (2, 8, 7) + 2e^- -> 2Cl^- (2, 8, 8)
3. Electrostatic Attraction:
   - The oppositely charged calcium cation (Ca^(2+)) and two chloride anions (2Cl^-) attract each other strongly via electrostatic forces of attraction, forming the neutral ionic compound calcium chloride (CaCl2).

iii. Dot and Cross Diagram of Calcium Chloride:
[ :Cl: (7 dots + 1 cross) ]^-   [ Ca ]^(2+)   [ :Cl: (7 dots + 1 cross) ]^-
(Or [Ca]^(2+) 2[:Cl:]^-)

questionText:
i. Define amorphous and crystalline solids. (2 Marks)
ii. Differentiate between gases and solids on the basis of the following properties. (5 Marks)
• Volume
• Compressibility
• Density
• Boiling point
• Ease of flow
sloText: Define amorphous and crystalline solids and compare the physical properties of gases and solids.
checkingHints: Part i (2 marks):
- Amorphous solids (1 mark): Solids in which particles are arranged randomly/irregularly without a definite 3D geometric shape or sharp melting point (e.g. glass, plastic, rubber).

- Crystalline solids (1 mark): Solids in which particles are arranged in a definite, orderly, repeating three-dimensional pattern resulting in definite geometric shapes and sharp melting points (e.g. diamond, NaCl).
Part ii (5 marks - 1 mark for each property comparison between gases and solids):
1. Volume: Gases have no fixed volume (expand to fill container); Solids have a definite, fixed volume.
2. Compressibility: Gases are highly compressible due to large empty intermolecular spaces; Solids are virtually incompressible due to tightly packed particles.
3. Density: Gases have very low density (expressed in g/dm3); Solids have high density (expressed in g/cm3).

4. Boiling point: Gases have very low (sub-zero) boiling points due to negligible intermolecular forces; Solids have very high melting and boiling points due to strong intermolecular/interionic forces.
5. Ease of flow: Gases flow easily and rapidly in all directions; Solids do not flow (particles only vibrate about fixed mean positions).

rubric.description: Part i: Defines amorphous solids (irregular particle arrangement, no sharp melting point).
Part i: Defines crystalline solids (ordered 3D lattice arrangement, sharp melting point).
Part ii: Differentiates gases and solids across Volume, Compressibility, Density, Boiling point, and Ease of flow (1 mark each).

modelAnswer:
i. Definitions:
- Amorphous Solids: Solids in which the constituent particles are not arranged in a regular, ordered pattern (irregular arrangement) and which lack a definite geometrical shape and sharp melting point (e.g., plastic, rubber, glass).
- Crystalline Solids: Solids in which the constituent atoms, ions, or molecules are arranged in a definite, regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern (crystal lattice), giving them definite geometrical shapes and sharp melting points (e.g., diamond, sodium chloride).

ii. Differentiation Between Gases and Solids:
1. Volume:
   - Gases: Do not have a fixed volume; gas molecules move freely and expand to occupy the entire available volume of their container.
   - Solids: Possess a definite, fixed volume because particles are locked in fixed positions.
2. Compressibility:
   - Gases: Are highly compressible because there are vast empty spaces between gas molecules.
   - Solids: Are incompressible because particles are tightly packed together with negligible intermolecular space.
3. Density:
   - Gases: Have very low density (typically measured in g/dm3, e.g., air = 0.0012 g/cm3) due to large volume and low mass per unit volume.
   - Solids: Have very high density (measured in g/cm3, e.g., Al = 2.7 g/cm3, Au = 19.3 g/cm3) because a large mass of particles is packed into a small volume.
4. Boiling Point:
   - Gases: Have very low boiling points (below room temperature) because intermolecular forces of attraction are extremely weak.
   - Solids: Have high melting and boiling points because strong intermolecular or interatomic forces require large thermal energy to overcome.
5. Ease of Flow:
   - Gases: Flow easily and rapidly in all directions due to negligible attractive forces and high translational kinetic energy.
   - Solids: Cannot flow at all because strong attractive forces restrict particles to vibrational motion about their fixed mean positions.

questionText:
The given diagram shows an electrolytic cell that is used for refining of copper.
i. Name the anode, cathode and electrolyte used for the given electrolytic cell. (3 Marks)
ii. How is copper purified through the process of electrolytic refining? Support your answer using balanced chemical equation for the reactions occurring at the anode and the cathode. (4 Marks)
sloText: Describe the electrolytic refining of copper including electrode materials, electrolyte, and half-cell reactions.
checkingHints: Part i (3 marks - 1 mark each):
- Anode: Impure / blistered copper block.
- Cathode: Thin sheet / plate of pure copper.
- Electrolyte: Aqueous copper(II) sulphate solution (CuSO4) acidified with dilute sulphuric acid (H2SO4).
Part ii (4 marks):

- Process explanation (2 marks): When electric current passes through the cell, copper atoms from the impure copper anode oxidise into Cu^(2+) ions and dissolve into the electrolyte (while insoluble impurities like Au and Ag settle at the bottom as anode mud). Cu^(2+) ions migrate to the pure copper cathode, gain electrons (reduce), and deposit as 99.99% pure copper metal.
- Anode half-equation (1 mark): Cu(s) [impure] -> Cu^(2+)(aq) + 2e^-
- Cathode half-equation (1 mark): Cu^(2+)(aq) + 2e^- -> Cu(s) [pure]

rubric.description: Part i: Identifies Anode as Impure (blistered) copper.
Part i: Identifies Cathode as Pure copper thin sheet/strip.
Part i: Identifies Electrolyte as acidified aqueous Copper(II) sulphate (CuSO4) solution.
Part ii: Explains dissolution of impure copper anode, migration of Cu^(2+) ions, deposition of pure copper on cathode, and settling of anode mud.
Part ii: Writes balanced anode oxidation equation: Cu -> Cu^(2+) + 2e^-.
Part ii: Writes balanced cathode reduction equation: Cu^(2+) + 2e^- -> Cu.

modelAnswer:
i. Components of the Electrolytic Cell for Refining Copper:
- Anode (Positive Electrode): Thick block of impure (blistered) copper.
- Cathode (Negative Electrode): Thin strip/sheet of pure copper metal.
- Electrolyte: Aqueous solution of copper(II) sulphate (CuSO4) acidified with a trace of dilute sulphuric acid (H2SO4).

ii. Process of Electrolytic Refining of Copper and Electrode Equations:
- Process Description:
  1. Impure copper plates (anodes) and thin pure copper sheets (cathodes) are suspended in an electrolytic tank filled with acidified copper(II) sulphate solution.
  2. When direct electric current (DC) is passed through the cell, metallic copper atoms from the impure anode lose two electrons each (undergo oxidation) and dissolve into the electrolyte as Cu^(2+) ions. As the anode dissolves away, less reactive metallic impurities such as silver (Ag) and gold (Au) fall to the bottom of the cell as valuable 'anode mud'.
  3. The positively charged Cu^(2+) ions from the electrolyte are attracted to the negatively charged pure copper cathode, where they gain two electrons each (undergo reduction) and deposit as a coating of 99.99% pure metallic copper.

- Balanced Chemical Equations:
  • At the Anode (Oxidation):
    Cu(s) (impure) -> Cu^(2+)(aq) + 2e^-
  • At the Cathode (Reduction):
    Cu^(2+)(aq) + 2e^- -> Cu(s) (pure deposit)
